results.result: IMC technology was validated for use on MS brain tissue by demonstrating that it reproduces immunofluorescence (IF) staining patterns with high correlation. The study performed two separate IMC runs: the first to validate the panel and approach, and the second to evaluate immune cell composition across lesion types. Significant positive correlations were found between IF and IMC for nuclei (r=0.9182, p=0.0002), CD3+ T cells (r=0.8929, p=0.01), PLP+ area (r=0.9544, p<0.0001), HLA+ cells (r=0.9794, p<0.0001), and CD68+ cells (r=0.9051, p<0.0001). The study concluded that IMC reproduces IF-equivalent staining patterns with cell lineage-specific markers expressed on appropriate cell types, and that antibodies validated with IF for MS brain studies will likely be applicable to IMC.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C44 provide strong statistical evidence (Spearman correlations with p<0.05 for all comparisons) demonstrating concordance between IF and IMC methods. The validation was performed systematically on serial sections with multiple markers (C34-C36), and the correlations are high (r>0.89 for all comparisons). The conclusion that IMC reproduces IF-equivalent patterns (C44, C52, C129) is well-supported by the quantitative data. The inference that IF-validated antibodies will be applicable to IMC (C130) is reasonable given the strong correlations, though the caveat about optimization (C131) is appropriately noted.

results.result: IMC enables discrimination of specific immune cell types in MS lesions using inclusion/exclusion criteria based on multiple markers. The technology successfully identified CD3+CD45+ T cells, CD3-CD45+CD68+ microglia/macrophages, κ+ or λ+ B cells (with appropriate allelic exclusion), CD31+collagen+ endothelial cells, and granzyme B+ cells. Specifically, IMC distinguished CD45high TMEM119-CD68+ macrophages from CD45low/+ TMEM119+CD68+ microglia, demonstrating the quantitative nature of the approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 provide specific examples of cell type identification with appropriate marker combinations, supported by Figure 2. The discrimination between macrophages and microglia (C134) using CD45 intensity and TMEM119 is a key technical achievement. The identification of B cells using κ/λ allelic exclusion (C48) provides internal validation of specificity. The detection of granzyme B (C51) demonstrates sensitivity for rare/low-abundance proteins. The claims about IMC's quantitative capabilities (C132-C133) are supported by the successful multi-marker discrimination.

results.result: IMC successfully differentiated between control white matter and various MS lesion stages in the NTZ rebound brain based on myelin (PLP) and microglia/macrophage (HLA) markers. Control white matter showed intact myelin with few HLA+ cells. Normal-appearing white matter (NAWM) in the NTZ rebound brain showed normal myelin but enriched HLA+ cells compared to control. (P)reactive lesions showed normal myelin with accumulated HLA+ cells. Active lesion cores showed loss of PLP signal with HLA+ cell accumulation. Mixed active-inactive lesions showed reduced myelin and HLA+ cell accumulation at the lesion edge. HLA+ cells containing PLP myelin products were found in both active lesions and at the edge of mixed active-inactive lesions, indicating demyelinating activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 describe qualitative observations of different lesion types supported by Figure 3. The progression from control (intact myelin, few HLA+ cells) through NAWM (normal myelin, more HLA+ cells) to active lesions (loss of myelin, many HLA+ cells) is logical and consistent with known MS pathology. The identification of HLA+ cells containing PLP (C58) provides direct evidence of active demyelination. The conclusion that IMC can differentiate lesion stages (C59) is supported by the distinct patterns observed across the different tissue types.

results.result: IMC revealed distinct microglial and macrophage phenotypes across MS lesion stages. In control white matter, TMEM119+ microglia showed ramified morphology with low/absent HLA, indicating a quiescent state, though some TMEM119+ microglia and TMEM119- macrophages showed activated phenotype (HLA+CD68+). In NTZ rebound NAWM, many TMEM119+ microglia were HLA+CD68+, unlike control. In (p)reactive lesions, TMEM119+ microglia accumulated with enlarged morphology and expressed HLA and CD68, along with TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ macrophages. Active lesions contained high numbers of TMEM119+HLA+CD68+ microglia and TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ macrophages with enlarged foamy morphology. The edge of mixed active-inactive lesions showed a rim of dense TMEM119+HLA+ microglia and TMEM119-HLA+ macrophages with enlarged CD68+ lysosomes, while the inactive core had few HLA+CD68+ cells with reduced HLA signal. Microglial activation was not restricted to lesional tissue but was also present in NAWM and (p)reactive lesion sites, where demyelinating blood-derived macrophages infiltrated the parenchyma despite normal-appearing myelination.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C72 provide detailed qualitative descriptions of microglial and macrophage phenotypes across lesion stages, supported by Figure 4. The progression from quiescent to activated states is well-documented with specific marker combinations (TMEM119, HLA, CD68) and morphological descriptions. The finding of microglial activation in NAWM (C66, C139) is consistent with prior literature (Zrzavy et al., 2017, cited in C139). The observation of demyelinating macrophages in NAWM with normal-appearing myelin (C140) is particularly interesting and supported by the data. The distinction between microglia and macrophages using TMEM119 is consistently applied throughout.

results.result: IMC characterized T cell phenotypes and activation states across MS lesion stages. In control white matter, CD3+CD8α- and CD3+CD8α+ T cells were rare or absent. In NAWM, some CD3+CD8α- and CD3+CD8α+ T cells were identified without signs of activation (NFAT1-). In (p)reactive lesions, both CD3+CD8α- and CD3+CD8α+ T cells were prominent but not activated (NFAT1-). Active lesions contained both T cell types, mostly in perivascular areas but also scattered in parenchyma, with some CD3+CD8α+ T cells showing activation (NFAT1+). At the edge of slowly expanding lesions, both T cell types were present, with some NFAT1+ cells found in both perivascular and parenchymal locations. The NFAT1 staining pattern was consistent with nuclear localization. Nuclear NFAT1 signal was also observed on CD3- cells, consistent with its expression in non-T cells. Ki67+ proliferating cells were occasionally observed, some of which were CD3+ T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C85 provide systematic characterization of T cell phenotypes across lesion stages, supported by Figure 5. The use of NFAT1 as an activation marker is appropriate and supported by citation (C75, Ma et al., 2015). The progression from absent/rare T cells in control to abundant T cells in lesions is well-documented. The observation that T cells in (p)reactive lesions are not activated (C76) despite being present is interesting and suggests they may not be driving early lesion formation. The detection of both perivascular and parenchymal T cells (C77, C81) addresses an important question about T cell localization. The observation of NFAT1 in CD3- cells (C83) is appropriately noted as consistent with literature.

results.result: IMC characterized B cell phenotypes across MS lesion stages using IgM, CD38, and κ/λ markers. In control white matter, IgM was found only in association with blood vessels (not with parenchymal Igκ/Igλ+ B cells), and the perivascular IgM signal co-localized with Igκ/Igλ, representing either naive/IgM memory B cells or cell-free immunoglobulins. In NAWM, IgM was found both in blood vessels and with nucleated Igκ/Igλ+ B cells in the parenchyma, and IgM- Igκ/Igλ+ B cells (class-switched) were also found in the parenchyma. In (p)reactive lesions, IgM was exclusively detected in blood vessels, and nucleated Igκ/Igλ+ B cells with switched phenotype (IgM-) were present. In active lesions and at the edge of mixed active-inactive lesions, nucleated Igκ/Igλ+ B cells with switched phenotype (IgM-) were mostly present.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C93 provide systematic characterization of B cell phenotypes across lesion stages, supported by Figure 6. The use of IgM, CD38, and κ/λ markers allows discrimination of naive, IgM memory, and class-switched B cells. The observation that IgM in control tissue is only perivascular (C86) while in NAWM it's also parenchymal (C88) suggests B cell infiltration. The predominance of class-switched B cells in lesions (C91-C93) is consistent with an ongoing adaptive immune response. The acknowledgment that perivascular IgM could represent either B cells or cell-free immunoglobulins (C87) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Quantitative IMC analysis revealed the distribution and phenotypes of demyelinating myeloid cells across lesion stages. In NAWM, a low density of demyelinating macrophages (CD45highHLA+TMEM-CD68+PLP+, 3 cells/mm²) was found. This increased drastically in (p)reactive lesions (34.8 cells/mm²), reaching peak density in active lesion cores (36.5 cells/mm²) and edges of active-inactive lesions (50.5 cells/mm²). Active cores also contained high density of non-demyelinating macrophages with empty vacuoles (CD45highHLA+TMEM-CD68+PLP-, 92.6 cells/mm²). Demyelinating microglia (CD45lowHLA+TMEM+CD68+PLP+) showed similar distribution with peak densities in active lesion cores (249.5 cells/mm²) and edges of active-inactive lesions (403.3 cells/mm²). Non-demyelinating microglia with empty vacuoles (CD45lowHLA+TMEM+CD68+PLP-) were found at high density in active cores (224.9 cells/mm²). In active lesion cores, 79% of HLA+ cells were microglia, constituting 87% of actively demyelinating phagocytes. At the edge of mixed active-inactive lesions, 88% of HLA+ cells were microglia, constituting 89% of actively demyelinating phagocytes. Macrophages infiltrating the parenchyma of active and mixed active-inactive lesions were largely inactive, indicated by enlarged but empty vacuoles.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 provide quantitative data on myeloid cell densities across lesion stages, supported by Figure 7a. The progression from low demyelinating activity in NAWM to peak activity in active lesions and active-inactive edges is logical and well-documented. The calculations showing that microglia constitute the majority (79-88%) of HLA+ cells and demyelinating phagocytes (87-89%) in active areas (C99-C100, C143) are important findings that challenge assumptions about the relative contributions of microglia vs. macrophages. The observation of non-demyelinating macrophages with empty vacuoles (C96, C144) is interpreted as representing phagocytes no longer actively demyelinating, which is reasonable but somewhat speculative regarding the mechanism (inability to digest myelin lipids, C145).

results.result: Quantitative IMC analysis revealed T cell distributions and activation states across lesion stages. Both CD8+ and CD4+ T cells were abundant from the (p)reactive stage onward, with peak densities in active lesion cores, periplaque, and rims of mixed active-inactive lesions. In active lesion cores, 60% of T cells were CD8+, with 3% activated and proliferating (NFAT+Ki67+). At the edge of mixed active-inactive lesions, 61% of T cells were CD4+, with 17% activated and proliferating (NFAT+Ki67+). Using an independent marker combination (CD38+HLA+), CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were enriched in active lesion cores and edges of active-inactive lesions, with CD4+CD38+HLA+ T cells particularly represented at active-inactive edges. Unlike NFAT+Ki67+ T cells, CD38+HLA+ T cells were present in particularly high density in (p)reactive lesions. An 'unclassified' T cell population (CD4+CD8+ or CD4-CD8-) was identified, present from the (p)reactive stage (11.2 cells/mm², 10% of T cells) with peak densities in active lesion cores (25.1 cells/mm², 21% of T cells) and rims of mixed active-inactive lesions (50.1 cells/mm², 31% of T cells). CD8+ T cells generally predominated across lesional stages and in some cases proliferated. A conspicuous number of CD4+ T cells were found not only in lesions but also at (p)reactive sites and periplaque white matter. CD4+CD38+HLA+ 'chronically activated' T cells were particularly abundant in (p)reactive lesion sites, suggesting involvement in early lesion formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C108 provide detailed quantitative data on T cell distributions, supported by Figure 7a. The use of two independent marker combinations (NFAT+Ki67+ and CD38+HLA+) for activation (C104-C106) strengthens the findings. The observation that CD4+ T cells predominate at active-inactive edges while CD8+ predominate in active cores (C102-C103) is interesting and suggests different roles. The identification of 'unclassified' T cells (C107-C108) is novel but requires further validation - the biological significance of CD4+CD8+ or CD4-CD8- T cells in this context is unclear. The interpretation that CD4+CD38+HLA+ T cells in (p)reactive lesions suggest involvement in early lesion formation (C150) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: Quantitative IMC analysis revealed B cell distributions across lesion stages. B cells were found across all lesion types, with switched memory B cells (CD45highIgκ/Igλ+IgM-CD38+) predominating in active lesion cores (29.2 cells/mm², 58% of B cells), periplaque white matter (22.2 cells/mm², 87% of B cells), and rims of mixed active-inactive lesions (44.0 cells/mm², 44% of B cells). The data reproduced immunohistological findings showing B lymphocytes in all lesion stages in lower numbers compared to T cells. The IMC panel using IgM, CD38, and κ/λ had increased capacity to identify different B cell subsets, including IgM+ and switched memory B cells, allowing better segregation of B cell phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 provides quantitative data on B cell distributions supported by Figure 7a. The predominance of switched memory B cells in active areas is consistent with an ongoing adaptive immune response. The comparison to prior immunohistological findings (C151) provides validation. The claim about increased capacity to identify B cell subsets (C152, C162) is supported by the use of multiple markers (IgM, CD38, κ/λ) that allow discrimination of naive, IgM memory, and class-switched B cells. However, the study acknowledges that additional markers (CD138, TACI) would be needed for full characterization of plasma cells (C163).

results.result: IMC distance analysis determined the spatial distribution of immune cells relative to blood vessels across lesion stages. Demyelinating macrophages infiltrated the parenchyma in (p)reactive lesions (136 μm from vessels) and periplaque white matter (131-191 μm), indicating demyelinating events in tissue without obvious demyelination. In active and active-inactive lesions, demyelinating macrophages were closer to vessels (87 μm and 70 μm, respectively). Non-demyelinating macrophages were found deeper in parenchyma of active (107 μm) and active-inactive lesions (244-279 μm). For T cells, both CD8+ and CD4+ infiltrated parenchyma in (p)reactive and periplaque areas (114-238 μm and 80-208 μm, respectively). At active-inactive edges and cores, CD4+ T cells were closer to vessels than CD8+ cells, which diffusely infiltrated parenchyma. In active lesions, CD8+ and CD4+ T cells equally infiltrated parenchyma (89 μm and 88 μm). For B cells, naive and switched memory B cells infiltrated parenchyma in (p)reactive lesions and periplaque white matter (62-113 μm). Within lesions, naive B cells were focally located in perivascular spaces at active-inactive edges and cores (2-9 μm), while switched memory B cells were near vessels at active-inactive edges/cores (19-44 μm) but diffusely infiltrated parenchyma of active lesions (82 μm).
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C118 provide detailed spatial analysis supported by Figure 7b. The observation that demyelinating macrophages are found deep in parenchyma of (p)reactive lesions and periplaque white matter (C110) is important as it indicates early demyelinating activity in apparently normal tissue. The differential localization of CD4+ vs. CD8+ T cells at active-inactive lesion edges (C114) is interesting and suggests different functional roles. The differential localization of naive vs. switched memory B cells (C117-C118) is also notable. However, the study acknowledges a limitation: blood vessels outside the imaged region could be missed (C158), which could affect distance measurements. The conclusion that IMC can determine which lymphocyte types reside closest to vessels (C4) is supported but with this caveat.

results.result: PHATE analysis of T cells revealed dynamics of T cell phenotypes across lesion types and locations. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells segregated into their own clusters, but a distinct cluster 't1' was identified containing CD4+, CD8+, and unassigned T cells, with unassigned T cells enriched in this cluster. Mixed active-inactive lesions were the most likely lesion type to contain cluster t1 cells. Cluster t1 cells were almost exclusively found close to blood vessels, whereas CD4+ and CD8+ T cells that discriminated from cluster t1 were farther from vessels. Cluster t1 cells had higher levels of CD45 and were less likely to have low levels of HLA (a marker of T cell exhaustion) but were not distinguishable from other lesion-resident cells in terms of Ki67, NFAT, or CD38 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C125 describe PHATE analysis results supported by Figure 8. The identification of a distinct T cell cluster (t1) enriched in mixed active-inactive lesions and located near blood vessels is interesting. However, several aspects are uncertain: (1) The biological significance of the 't1' cluster is unclear - it contains a mix of CD4+, CD8+, and 'unassigned' T cells, making interpretation difficult. (2) The 'unassigned' T cells (CD4+CD8+ or CD4-CD8-) identified earlier (C107-C108) are of uncertain biological relevance and may represent technical artifacts (e.g., doublets, cells with intermediate marker expression). (3) The PHATE analysis is performed on a single patient case, limiting generalizability. (4) The functional significance of the t1 cluster's proximity to blood vessels and higher CD45/HLA expression is speculative. While the analysis demonstrates IMC's capability for high-dimensional analysis, the biological interpretation requires validation in additional samples.

results.result: The study provides background on MS pathology and identifies a gap in the field. MS is characterized by heterogeneous demyelinated and inflammatory lesions in the CNS. Lesions are staged into categories including NAWM, (p)reactive lesions, PPWM, active demyelinating lesions, mixed active/inactive lesions, and inactive lesions. Demyelination patterns vary (I: T cell-mediated; II: IgG/complement-mediated; III/IV: oligodendrocyte dystrophy). Lymphocytes, microglia, and macrophages are associated with active demyelination and play key roles in disease. Microglia and macrophages can acquire pro-inflammatory phenotypes. T cells (CD8+ and CD4+) and B cells are found in lesions with various phenotypes and activation states. While past immunohistological studies provided insights, they are limited by the number of analytes that can be simultaneously visualized on a tissue section. Thus, a comprehensive analysis of single-cell phenotypes and functional states in relation to demyelination within MS tissue is lacking.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C27 provide established background knowledge about MS pathology, supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. The description of lesion staging (C8), demyelination patterns (C10-C12), and roles of various immune cells (C13-C25) is consistent with current understanding of MS. The identification of a gap in the field (C28) - lack of comprehensive single-cell analysis due to limitations of traditional immunohistology (C27) - provides clear rationale for the study. These claims are well-supported by citations and represent accurate summaries of prior work.

results.result: The study describes IMC technology, its application to a specific MS case, and discusses its potential and limitations. IMC uses time-of-flight inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry to detect dozens of markers simultaneously by measuring metal isotopes tagged to antibodies. The study analyzed staged lesions in a case with severe rebound MS disease activity after natalizumab cessation, which serves as a good positive control due to its highly inflammatory nature. IMC has advantages (multiplexing capability) but also limitations (low throughput, yields information only about imaged regions, single case study). The study's goal was to provide proof that IMC can be used for analysis of complex cellular phenotypes in heterogeneous tissues like MS brain, with future directions to apply the technique to well-characterized MS brain tissue cohorts. The data reproduced immunohistological patterns previously described in carefully staged MS lesions. The authors propose that IMC will enable high-dimensional analysis of single-cell phenotypes, functional states, and cell-cell interactions in relation to lesion morphometry and demyelinating activity, and has potential to profoundly impact knowledge of inflammatory response and tissue injury in MS brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 describe IMC technology and study rationale, supported by appropriate citations (C30, C31). The selection of the NTZ rebound case as a positive control (C32) is reasonable given its highly inflammatory nature. Claims C165-C177 discuss advantages, limitations, and future directions. The acknowledgment of limitations (C166-C169: low throughput, limited to imaged regions, single case) is appropriate and honest. The statement that the study provides 'proof of concept' (C170) rather than definitive findings is accurate given the single-case design. The proposals about IMC's potential (C176-C177) are reasonable extrapolations from the demonstrated capabilities. The claim that data reproduced prior immunohistological patterns (C175) is supported by the validation experiments and consistency with cited literature.

results.result: The study discusses technical considerations, prior findings, and areas of uncertainty. Antibody optimization may be required for IMC (titration/amplification). Microglial activation in control brain is consistent with prior studies showing expression of activation markers and lack of P2RY12 in 48% of control microglia, though the cause (infections, aging, inherent property) is unclear. The presence of enlarged empty vacuoles in macrophages is likely due to inability to digest myelin lipids. Prior studies suggest CD8+ T cells show tissue-resident memory features and B cells are restricted to perivascular spaces, with the possibility that demyelination is induced by soluble factors from lymphocytes. The current study observed both perivascular and parenchymal localization of lymphocytes, but blood vessels outside imaged regions could be missed. Further analysis is required to determine if parenchymal lymphocytes are a generalized MS feature. B cell characterization in MS tissue is lacking, though recent clinical studies show protective effects of anti-CD20 therapies. Additional markers (CD138, TACI) are needed for full B cell characterization. Some B lineage cells may play protective roles in neuroinflammation.
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately discuss technical considerations (C131), place findings in context of prior work (C136-C137, C153-C155, C161, C164), acknowledge uncertainties (C138, C158-C160), and identify areas for future work (C159, C163). The discussion of microglial activation in control brain (C136-C138) appropriately cites relevant literature and acknowledges uncertainty about mechanisms. The speculation about macrophage vacuoles (C145) and lymphocyte-derived soluble factors (C156) are reasonable but clearly presented as interpretations. The acknowledgment of limitations in lymphocyte localization analysis (C158) and need for additional markers (C163) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The study describes the patient case and control used. The patient was a 32-year-old female with relapsing-remitting MS diagnosed in 2005. Natalizumab therapy was initiated but stopped after 2 years due to JCV antibody positivity, despite clinical/radiological stability. Four months after cessation, the patient was hospitalized with new deficits and worsened over 2 weeks (EDSS 9.5), developing new gadolinium-enhancing lesions despite methylprednisolone treatment. Autopsy was performed within 1 hour post-mortem. Pathologic analysis revealed abundant, active demyelinating, highly inflammatory MS lesions with pattern II (IgG- and complement-mediated). Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and IRIS were excluded pathologically, though a later study proposed EBV-associated IRIS as a possible cause. IHC and qPCR for JCV were negative. The diagnosis was severe MS rebound inflammatory demyelinating activity after NTZ withdrawal. The control was an 86-year-old female who died of cardiac arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C189 provide detailed clinical and pathological information about the patient case, supported by citations to prior publications (C31, C184, C186, C188). The case represents a well-characterized example of NTZ rebound disease with extensive pathological documentation. The acknowledgment of alternative interpretations (EBV-associated IRIS, C186) while noting the original pathological diagnosis excluded IRIS (C185) demonstrates appropriate scientific nuance. The control case description (C189) is brief but adequate. This case selection is appropriate for the study's proof-of-concept goals, though the single-case limitation is acknowledged elsewhere (C169).
